findings.title: Live RLS hole: an orphaned permissive UPDATE policy neutralizes every later restriction on reviews
findings.principle: When a new, more restrictive RLS policy is added to replace overly-permissive write access on a table, the migration that adds it must DROP the old permissive policy for the same command in the same migration, and this must be verified by a one-time query (not a memory) confirming exactly one permissive policy remains per (table, command) pair unless the OR-combination is a deliberate, named design. Postgres RLS combines multiple PERMISSIVE policies for the same command with OR, so an old USING(true) policy is never narrowed by a newer, stricter one added later; it must be explicitly retired.
findings.why: Postgres evaluates all applicable PERMISSIVE policies for a command as an OR: a row passes if ANY one of them allows it. A team that reasons 'we tightened this with a new policy' without checking for surviving old ones ships a control that looks fixed in code review (the diff shows a new, correct policy) while being unfixed in the database (the old catch-all is still live and wins the OR). This is exactly the same 'looks wired, does nothing' failure class this project has already named as its number one problem (silent no-ops), just at the DDL layer instead of the query layer, which is why it is invisible to code review and to every grep that only looks at the newest migration.
findings.local_evidence: supabase/migrations/005_reviews_trust.sql:29-31 creates `CREATE POLICY IF NOT EXISTS "Owners can update review replies" ON reviews FOR UPDATE USING (true) WITH CHECK (true);` with no TO clause (applies to every role Postgres grants UPDATE to on this table, which by Supabase's default bootstrap GRANTs is both anon and authenticated). supabase/migrations/029_review_policies.sql:4-7 later adds the intended real restriction, `CREATE POLICY "reviews_update_own_48h" ON public.reviews FOR UPDATE USING (auth.uid() = user_id AND created_at > now() - interval '48 hours')`, clearly meant to be the actual rule (own review, 48h window). Because Postgres ORs permissive policies, the 005 policy still applies and its USING/WITH CHECK are both `true`, so the 029 restriction is decorative: any client holding a valid anon or authenticated Supabase key can UPDATE any column (rating, review text, is_flagged, booking_id, owner_reply, etc.) on ANY row of the reviews table for ANY salon, via a direct PostgREST call that never touches this app's route handlers at all. _design-system/REMOVED.md's 2026-07-25 entry ('reviews-reply-route...') confirms the APP-layer write path to owner_reply/salon_response was already retired as dead, which the owner may have believed closed this surface; it did not, because the vulnerable object is the table-wide RLS policy, not the app route, and the policy was never touched by that cleanup.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'DROP POLICY.*reviews\|ALTER POLICY.*reviews' supabase/migrations/*.sql -> only three DROPs found ("Users can insert reviews", "Salon owners can update reviews", "Public can insert reviews", plus an ALTER POLICY on reviews_insert_own), none of them the FOR UPDATE USING(true) policy named 'Owners can update review replies'. grep -rn 'GRANT.*reviews\|ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES' supabase/migrations/*.sql -> zero hits, confirming no repo migration narrows the Supabase-default anon/authenticated table grants that make this RLS policy the only backstop. grep -ri 'orphaned polic\|permissive.*OR\|multiple permissive' _backend-system _docs _rules -> zero hits; the research/authz.md file discusses RLS extensively (326 CREATE POLICY statements counted) but never checks for this specific class of bug (a superseded-in-intent-but-not-in-fact policy).
findings.existing_coverage: none: research/authz.md section 3-4 covers IDOR and tenant isolation as prose principles but was written from a table/policy COUNT (326 CREATE POLICY statements exist) never from a per-table, per-command AUDIT of what those policies actually combine to allow. No gate, lint, or checklist item checks for more than one permissive policy per (table, command).
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md (once created) as a named RLS-authoring rule under the authz section, plus an immediate one-off remediation: DROP the 005_reviews_trust.sql policy in a new migration and re-verify against the live DB with a query grouping pg_policies by (tablename, cmd) having count(*) > 1.
findings.enforcement: gate: a script (could reuse the project's own `npm run exists`-style tooling or a small python script) that queries pg_policies (or greps all migrations for CREATE POLICY ... FOR <cmd>) and fails when a table has more than one PERMISSIVE policy for the same command unless the pair is listed in an explicit allowlist naming why the OR is intentional. Also runnable as a one-time manual audit before it becomes a script.

findings.title: The `staff` role is authorization-unmodeled at every layer and is actively locked out of the surface it exists for
findings.principle: Every value in profiles.role must have a written authorization invariant, enforced identically at the route/middleware layer and the RLS layer, before any UI or invite flow that grants that role ships. A role that can be assigned to a user but has no corresponding RLS predicate and no route-layer allowlist is not a smaller version of another role, it is an unenforced no-op, and the system must fail the invite flow (or route it into an existing modeled role) rather than mint an unenforceable identity.
findings.why: An authorization model is not the union of every role name that appears in a column comment; it is the set of roles that have an actual, checkable predicate somewhere. A role that exists in the schema and in an onboarding flow but nowhere in the enforcement layer is worse than no role at all: it creates a false sense that a permission boundary exists ('staff have restricted access') when the real boundary is binary (dashboard reachable or not), and the eventual fix is discovered by a real staff member hitting a wall, not by anyone reading a spec.
findings.local_evidence: middleware.ts:175 and :193 gate the entire /{locale}/dashboard/** tree on `role !== "salon_owner" && role !== "admin"` with no third branch for `staff`; a profile with role='staff' is redirected to the homepage on every dashboard route, full stop. app/api/staff/accept-invite/route.ts:111-114 sets `staff_salon_id` on a profile as the terminal step of an invite-acceptance flow, producing exactly the account shape middleware.ts locks out. staff_members.permissions (a jsonb/array column, see supabase/migrations/20260706083518_restrict_staff_sensitive_cols_and_pin_search_path.sql:7, which only REVOKEs anon SELECT on it, never defines what it gates) is read in exactly one file, app/api/staff/my-schedule/route.ts:75, and written from one settings UI, app/[locale]/dashboard/staff/page.tsx:79-80 -- neither reads it to grant or deny anything, it is stored and displayed, not enforced. Zero RLS policies in any migration reference staff_salon_id (grep below). Of 357 route.ts files, exactly 1 (app/api/salon/setup-progress/route.ts) contains the literal string 'staff' as a role check.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'staff_salon_id' supabase/migrations/*.sql | grep -i 'policy\|using\|with check' -> zero hits (the only migration hit for staff_salon_id at all is the ALTER TABLE that adds the column, 069_megabuild_staff.sql:30). grep -rl '"staff"' app/api -> 1 file. grep -rn 'CREATE TABLE.*permission' supabase/migrations/*.sql -> zero hits (no dedicated staff_permissions table exists despite the CLAUDE.md project memory naming 'per-staff perms' as part of the locked dashboard rebuild spec). grep -ri 'staff.*authoriz\|staff.*permission.*model\|staff.*invariant' _backend-system _docs _rules -> only research/authz.md mentions it, and only as a forward-looking caveat ('staff-to-salon access is genuinely unmodeled... a gap already visible today'), never as a resolved decision.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: research/authz.md section 1 and 'Premature at our scale' both name staff-to-salon access as the one real gap in Solen's RBAC-plus-RLS-ownership model and correctly flag it as NOT yet a ReBAC-shaped problem (a staff member belongs to exactly one salon today, one hop, RBAC-plus-ownership is still the right shape). It does not, however, say what should happen to staff RIGHT NOW: the research stops at 'this is unmodeled' and does not resolve the middleware contradiction (a role that exists but is banned from the surface it was created for).
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md under authz, plus an actual code fix: either (a) middleware.ts adds a staff branch scoped to a small, explicit allowlist of dashboard subpaths (their own booking calendar, their own schedule) with an RLS predicate on staff_salon_id backing every one of those tables, or (b) the product decision is made explicit that staff accounts are not live yet and accept-invite should not silently produce an unreachable account (surface an error or a 'coming soon' state instead).
findings.enforcement: gate: none exists today and none is proposed as urgent at 28 salons (this is a product-completeness gap more than an attack surface, since the failure mode is 'staff locked out', not 'staff over-privileged'). checklist: any future PR that adds a new profiles.role value must include a corresponding RLS policy AND a middleware/route allowlist entry before merge, verified by the reviewer, not a script, given how rarely new roles are added.

findings.title: No gate checks object-level (IDOR/BOLA) authorization; the one authz-adjacent gate only checks that SOME auth call exists
findings.principle: A route that accepts a client-supplied object id (a path param or body field ending in _id, or a bare id, that is used in a WHERE/eq/match against a privileged table) must, in the same file, load that row and assert the caller's identity against an ownership or scope column (owner_id, user_id, salon_id via a join, staff_salon_id) before performing the privileged read or write. Passing an authentication check (a valid, logged-in getUser()) is necessary but never sufficient proof that this happened, and no gate should treat it as sufficient.
findings.why: OWASP's own API Security Top 10 has ranked Broken Object Level Authorization #1 in both its 2019 and 2023 editions specifically because this exact substitution, 'the user is logged in, therefore the request is authorized', is the most common real API bug: a role check answers a coarse question the code CAN get right while still leaking a horizontal check the code got wrong for one specific row. A codebase that only gates on 'is there an auth signal in this file' will pass code review and pass its own hook while shipping a route that updates any booking by id regardless of whose it is, because 'getUser() is present' says nothing about what happens after it.
findings.local_evidence: /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks/no-unauth-money-route.py is the only hook in the estate that inspects authorization shape on a new route, and its own docstring states its AUTH_SIGNALS list is deliberately just presence checks: 'auth.getUser(', 'requireAdmin(', 'CRON_SECRET', 'applyRateLimit', etc, with an explicit comment that a bare Supabase client was REMOVED from the signal list precisely because 'it must co-occur with an actual session read... to count' -- but the gate stops at session read, it never inspects whether the file also checks the object id against an ownership column. A route can satisfy this gate completely (calls getUser(), is logged in) while still doing `admin.from('bookings').update({...}).eq('id', bodyBookingId)` with zero ownership predicate, and nothing in this repo's tooling would flag it. Of 357 route.ts files, 236 call getUser() but only 96 reference owner_id anywhere in the file (a rough proxy, not a precise count, since many of those 96 overlaps are legitimately public-salon-lookup routes that read owner_id for display, not for a check) -- the gap between 236 and 96 is not itself proof of vulnerable routes, but it is proof that no tooling distinguishes 'authenticated' routes that also perform an object check from ones that don't.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rli 'BOLA\|IDOR' _rules _design-system CLAUDE.md .claude/hooks /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks -> the only three hits (scale-excuse-gate.py, fable-skill-trigger.py, backend-doc-pointer.py) are topic-routing hooks that mention the term to trigger the fable-backend SKILL load, none of them actually check for the pattern in code. grep -ri 'object.level\|ownership check' .claude/hooks /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks -> zero hits in any hook body (only in the research prose). ls .claude/hooks | grep -i 'auth\|owner\|idor' -> exactly one file, no-getsession-authz-gate.py, which checks a completely different thing (getSession vs getUser, not object-level authorization at all).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: research/authz.md section 3 states the principle correctly and in detail (T1, OWASP API1:2023) and names the exact Solen instance already documented in _docs/BACKEND.md (the availability_slots/bookings RLS-client trap). What is missing is the enforcement half: the research recommends the rule but nothing checks that a NEW route actually follows it, and the one gate that touches this area (no-unauth-money-route.py) explicitly only checks for authentication presence, not the object check.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md authz section (the invariant, verbatim, with the threshold: 'every route reading params.id / body.*_id against a privileged table must .eq() or join an ownership column before the privileged operation'), and a project hook alongside no-unauth-money-route.py.
findings.enforcement: gate: extend .claude/hooks (project-level, since it needs the repo's own table/column shape) with a heuristic check: a new route.ts under app/api that destructures a client-supplied id AND performs an .update()/.delete()/.select() with sensitive fields against a known privileged table (bookings, salons, reviews, staff_members, profiles) must also contain an ownership-shaped predicate (owner_id, user_id, staff_salon_id, or an explicit requireX helper) in the same file, else warn (not hard-block, since false positives on genuinely public routes are likely at first) until the false-positive rate is known.

findings.title: Deep authorization research exists for both authn and authz, but nothing is frozen into law, and the authz audit was never written
findings.principle: A researched-but-unfrozen decision does not bind a future session; only a dated row in LAW.md does. Before any authz-adjacent PR is merged, _backend-system/LAW.md must contain a frozen row for: the RBAC-plus-RLS-ownership model choice, where an authorization check must live (route handler AND RLS, never middleware alone), the object-level-check requirement, and the service-role-escape-hatch discipline, each citing its research section and tier. Until LAW.md exists, treat research/authz.md's 'Decision candidates' table as the interim answer, but say so explicitly rather than silently re-deriving a decision from a fresh reading of the research prose every session.
findings.why: The entire _backend-system/ folder was built, per its own README, because 'it keeps making stuff up when I open a new session' -- research alone does not solve that problem, because a 171-line prose file with nine points, five sections, a decision table and a myths section is still something a fresh session has to re-read and re-interpret in full before it can act, and interpretation is exactly where drift and invention happen. A LAW.md with one locked row per axis is the only artifact that lets a session answer 'what do we do about X' in one lookup instead of a re-derivation.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/ contains README.md, audit/, and research/ only (ls confirmed); LAW.md, RATIONALE.md, AUDIT_2026-07-16.md and QUESTIONS.md, all four files the README's own layer-map table promises at the folder root, do not exist. _backend-system/audit/ contains 8 files (api-design.md, authn.md, backup-recovery.md, file-storage.md, jobs-async.md, migrations.md, transactions-concurrency.md, webhooks.md) -- authz.md is not among them, so even the 'did we verify we follow the researched authz law' pass (which authn.md got, with a full per-principle MATCH/PARTIAL/GAP table and two confirmed HIGH findings) was never done for authorization at all, despite authz being research/authz.md's own stated #1 concern ('the single most important fact for this codebase').
findings.absence_proof: find _backend-system -iname 'LAW.md' -o -iname 'RATIONALE.md' -> zero hits. ls _backend-system/audit/ -> authz.md absent from the 8 files present. grep -ri 'authorization invariant\|authz invariant' _backend-system _docs _rules _design-system CLAUDE.md /Users/sulo/.claude/*.md /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks .claude/hooks -> zero hits anywhere in the estate outside this finding's own phrasing.
findings.existing_coverage: none for the freeze itself; the research (research/authz.md, 171 lines, 9-point short version, 5 detailed sections, a decision-candidates table, myths, premature-at-scale, and unverified sections) is thorough and already does the analytical work LAW.md would just need to compress into locked rows.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md and _backend-system/audit/authz.md, both net-new files, mirroring the shape audit/authn.md already demonstrates works (verdict paragraph, coverage+method section, per-principle MATCH/PARTIAL/GAP/UNKNOWN table with file:line evidence, gaps-in-detail, what's-right section, unknowns).

findings.title: 270 service-role call sites carry the entire authorization decision by hand, with zero audit of which ones actually have the required adjacent check
findings.principle: Every createAdminSupabaseClient() call site must have, in the same function, an explicit and visibly-commented ownership/role assertion immediately before the privileged query it protects, because BYPASSRLS means the database enforces nothing at all for that connection. A periodic (not one-time) sampling audit of a fixed fraction of call sites (for example 10% per quarter, or all NEW call sites added since the last audit) must confirm this holds, because the count only grows as the codebase grows and prose-only discipline decays under time pressure.
findings.why: The service-role key maps to a Postgres role with the BYPASSRLS attribute, which is not a client-library setting that degrades gracefully, it is a hard database-level bypass evaluated per-connection regardless of what headers, comments, or intentions the calling code carries. Once a query runs on that connection, the database's own defense-in-depth layer (RLS, which this project's own research correctly calls its 'real enforcement layer') contributes nothing; the entire authorization decision for that call collapses onto whatever a human remembered to type in application code, and 270 independent, unaudited places for that memory to fail is a materially larger attack surface than every RLS policy gap combined, by the research's own reasoning.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rl createAdminSupabaseClient app lib returns 270 files (this session's own count; research/authz.md's earlier count of 267 is close enough to confirm it is not shrinking). A quick heuristic sweep this session (files with createAdminSupabaseClient but no getUser()/owner_id/role check/CRON_SECRET/webhook-signature pattern anywhere in the same file) flagged 71 files; spot-checking two of them (app/api/bookings/[id]/dispute/route.ts, app/api/directory/[id]/claim/route.ts) showed the check is real but funneled through a shared helper (resolveBookingActor()) my grep pattern missed, so the true unchecked count is unknown, not zero and not 71 -- exactly the situation an unaudited surface produces: nobody, including this research pass, can currently state the real number with confidence.
findings.absence_proof: research/authz.md's own 'Unverified' section states plainly: 'this file establishes the COUNT... and the documented INVARIANT... but does not claim to have audited each one for compliance; that is future audit work.' No file, migration, hook, or CI script in this repo performs that audit. grep -rn 'createAdminSupabaseClient' .claude/hooks /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks -> zero hits, confirming no gate inspects new admin-client call sites at all.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the invariant itself is written down twice (research/authz.md section 6, and _docs/BACKEND.md:153, quoted directly in the research: 'the admin client does no authorization by itself... RLS provides zero protection once you're on the service-role client'). What is missing is any verification that the invariant is actually followed, at any point in time, for any subset of the 270 sites.
findings.where_it_should_live: a dedicated audit pass (not a research file, an actual line-by-line review) tracked the same way _plans/*_AUDIT.md files track other findings, plus a lighter-weight ongoing gate for new call sites.
findings.enforcement: gate: a new project hook that fires on Write/Edit introducing a new createAdminSupabaseClient( call and requires an ownership/role-check pattern (owner_id, .role, requireX(, or a named resolver like resolveBookingActor() / resolveBookingActor-shaped helper) to appear in the same file, warn-only at first given the false-positive risk from helper indirection observed in this session's spot check. Separately, a one-time manual sampling audit (e.g. 30-40 of the 270 files, weighted toward routes that mutate money or PII) to establish a real baseline number, since the current number is genuinely unknown, not just uncounted.

findings.title: Several tables carry unscoped WITH CHECK (true) INSERT policies that let a direct PostgREST caller bypass all app-layer business logic
findings.principle: An INSERT policy on a table whose rows carry a salon_id, staff_id, or price/amount field must scope WITH CHECK to that identity (auth.uid() = user_id, or an EXISTS check against the owning salon/staff), never WITH CHECK (true), unless the table is genuinely intended to accept anonymous, unscoped writes (a newsletter signup, a public contact form) and that intent is stated in a comment on the policy itself.
findings.why: The app's own API routes are not the only path to the database once a Supabase anon or authenticated key exists client-side; anyone can call PostgREST directly with that same key. An unscoped WITH CHECK (true) INSERT policy means every business rule the app enforces in TypeScript (a booking's price matches the service's real price, an inventory row belongs to the salon that owns it, a staff calendar entry belongs to the staff member who owns it) is opt-in for a legitimate client and completely absent for a client that skips the app and calls the database directly, which is a normal, unprivileged thing to do with a public anon key, not an exotic attack.
findings.local_evidence: grep found FOR INSERT WITH CHECK (true) (no scoping predicate) still live and never dropped on at least: bookings (001_booking_reviews.sql, 'Public can insert bookings'), salon_photos (004_salon_photos.sql, 'Authenticated users can insert salon photos'), addons (006_bleaching_addons.sql, 'Auth insert addons'), inventory (005_dashboard_upgrades.sql, 'Auth insert inventory'), sms_reminders and staff_calendars (005_dashboard_upgrades.sql), loyalty_stamps (039_loyalty.sql, 'loyalty_stamps_insert_system'), and quartier_subscriptions (064_quartier_subscriptions.sql). Some of these (quartier_subscriptions, a public newsletter-style signup) are legitimately unscoped by design; others (inventory, staff_calendars, addons) attach to a specific salon or staff member and have no predicate tying the inserted row's salon_id/staff_id to the caller at all, meaning any authenticated user (any customer with a normal login) can insert an inventory row, a staff calendar entry, or an addon definition under ANY salon's id via a direct PostgREST call.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'WITH CHECK (true)' supabase/migrations/*.sql | wc -l -> part of 54 total USING(true)/WITH CHECK(true) hits across the codebase; grep -B4 for the CREATE POLICY context on each isolates the write ones from the (mostly legitimate) public-SELECT ones. grep -rn 'DROP POLICY.*inventory\|DROP POLICY.*staff_calendars\|DROP POLICY.*addons' supabase/migrations/*.sql -> zero hits, confirming none of these were later scoped or retired the way some reviews policies were.
findings.existing_coverage: none; research/authz.md's 326-CREATE-POLICY count is a count, not an audit of what those 326 policies actually restrict, and no existing doc distinguishes 'this table is meant to be publicly insertable' from 'this table looks scoped-by-app-code but has no database-level scoping at all.'
findings.where_it_should_live: the same one-time RLS audit named in authz-rls-01 (a full pg_policies review, not just a count), grouped by table and annotated with intended scope; the fix for each finding is either a narrower WITH CHECK or an explicit 'intentionally public' comment on the policy.
findings.enforcement: gate: extend the eventual permissive-policy-count check (authz-rls-01's enforcement) to also flag any WITH CHECK (true) / USING (true) on a table whose schema includes a salon_id, staff_id, owner_id, or user_id column, since the presence of that column is itself strong evidence the table was meant to be scoped.

findings.title: RLS's silent-zero-rows failure mode has no enforcement in authorization-sensitive writes despite three confirmed prior incidents
findings.principle: Every write (.update()/.delete()) against a privileged table, whether issued on the session client or the admin client, must check the actual number of affected rows (via .select() after the write, or checking the returned array length / count) and treat zero rows as an explicit failure path, never as an implicit success. This binds hardest on writes gated by RLS ownership predicates, because a zero-row result there is indistinguishable, from the response alone, between 'correctly refused an unauthorized caller' and 'silently failed to do the authorized thing.'
findings.why: PostgREST (and by extension Supabase's client libraries) returns error: null for an UPDATE/DELETE that matched zero rows, which is a database-correct response (no error occurred) but an application-dangerous one, because the two possible causes of zero rows, a bug and a security boundary working as intended, look byte-for-byte identical to code that only checks the error field. This is a generic Postgres/PostgREST fact, not a Solen quirk, but it is uniquely dangerous in authorization-sensitive paths because the outcome that would normally be user-visible (an error, a 403) is instead swallowed and the caller can proceed believing a write happened.
findings.local_evidence: This exact class is already documented as having bitten Solen three times: availability_slots writes from a non-owner session client (slots_manage_owner policy, per _docs/BACKEND.md), bookings rollback deletes at app/api/bookings/route.ts:541,549,554 routing through the session client instead of the documented claimSlot() admin-client helper (flagged, unresolved, in _docs/BACKEND.md section 2), and a now-fixed instance on group_bookings (_plans/BOOKING_BACKEND_AUDIT.md:187, closed by two migrations). Three confirmed live incidents of the identical failure shape is a pattern, not a one-off bug.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'affected.row\|row.count\|rowCount' .claude/hooks /Users/sulo/.claude/hooks -> zero hits; no gate inspects a new .update()/.delete() call for a row-count check. The project's own no-getsession-authz-gate.py proves the pattern (a hook that blocks a specific dangerous API shape) is workable here; nothing analogous exists for the update-without-row-count-check shape despite it having a longer, better-documented incident history in this specific codebase than the getSession() issue did at the time that gate was built.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the CLAUDE.md project instructions already name this as the project's '#1 silent failure mode' in general (the Silent no-ops section) and research/authz.md's Myths and traps section restates it specifically for authorization writes. The gap is purely enforcement: it is repeated as advice in at least three places and has caused three confirmed incidents, which is precisely the 'advice gets outranked under task focus, a gate does not' pattern this project's own /harden methodology exists to fix, yet no such gate has been built for this specific, well-evidenced case.
findings.where_it_should_live: a project hook alongside no-getsession-authz-gate.py and no-unauth-money-route.py.
findings.enforcement: gate: a heuristic PreToolUse check on new/edited route.ts and lib/**.ts files: an .update(/.delete( call against a table not immediately followed (within the same statement chain or the next few lines) by a .select() and a check of the result's length, or an explicit comment naming why the row count doesn't matter for this call, gets flagged. Given the false-positive risk (many updates legitimately don't need this, e.g. best-effort/non-critical writes), warn rather than hard-block, scoped to routes already known to touch bookings/availability_slots/group_bookings or any table with an ownership-scoped RLS policy.

findings.title: No differentiated authorization tier exists for the owner/staff dashboard session versus a browsing customer session, despite its documented adjacency to Stripe Connect payouts
findings.principle: A session that can reach the salon-owner or staff dashboard (one hop from Stripe Connect payout control and from other customers' PII) must require re-authentication (a fresh password/MFA check, not just a valid existing session) before the highest-blast-radius actions specifically: changing the connected Stripe payout account, changing the account email/password, or granting a new staff invite. This is a stricter bar than 'is this session currently valid', and it is currently the same bar as a customer browsing salons.
findings.why: Not every authenticated session carries the same risk if compromised. A stolen customer session can see one person's bookings; a stolen salon-owner session sits adjacent to money movement (payouts) and other customers' contact data, so the cost of a false negative (an attacker with a stolen owner session doing real damage before anyone notices) is categorically higher, and the cost of a false positive (an owner having to re-enter a password once before changing bank details) is categorically lower than the cost to a customer of the same friction on every login. Treating all four roles as equally risky because they run through identical authentication code is optimizing for code simplicity over the actual blast-radius shape of the product.
findings.local_evidence: middleware.ts's dashboard gate (lines 148-224) checks role once per request and applies the identical session-validity bar to every dashboard route, from a staff calendar view to (if the feature existed) a payout-account change; there is no step-up/reauth call anywhere in app/api/dashboard/** or app/api/staff/** (grepped, zero hits for a password-confirmation or MFA-challenge pattern in any dashboard-adjacent route). Solen's own Stripe Connect payout wiring (app/api/tips/route.ts:142, app/api/walkin/tip/route.ts:160, per research/authz.md's own Stripe trap) already routes real money through stripeAccountId read off the salons row, so the adjacency this principle is about is not hypothetical, it's already live.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'reauthenticat\|step.up\|confirm.*password' app/api/dashboard app/api/staff app/api/salon -> zero hits. grep -ri 'session tier\|blast radius\|owner.*dashboard.*mfa' _backend-system _docs _rules -> only research/authn.md's own trap list mentions this exact idea ('OUR STACK'S TRAP #4... any AuthN hardening priority call should weight this tier higher'), stated as a prioritization note for future MFA work, never as a standalone, actionable authz rule for reauth-on-sensitive-action independent of MFA.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: research/authn.md section 10 recommends MFA specifically for the owner/staff tier (a related but distinct control, since MFA guards LOGIN, not a mid-session sensitive action) and its trap #4 names the blast-radius asymmetry in passing. Neither research file states a reauth-on-sensitive-action rule as its own line item.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md authz section, and eventually a small requireReauth() helper analogous to lib/auth/require.ts, called from the specific sensitive routes once they exist (there is no live payout-account-change route yet per this session's search, so this is a 'build it right when built' item, not a live gap to patch today).
findings.enforcement: checklist for now (a payout-account-change or staff-invite-permission-grant route does not exist yet to gate); once one is built, gate: require a requireReauth()-shaped call in the same route.

findings.title: FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is confirmed absent on every table, and the session-client's Postgres role identity has never been checked
findings.principle: Verify once, and record the answer as law rather than as an open question: which Postgres role does the Supabase 'authenticated'/'anon' session-client connection actually run as, and does that role own any table it's supposed to be RLS-restricted on. If (as is virtually certain for a standard Supabase project) the session client never runs as the table owner, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is moot for app traffic and the law should say so explicitly, closing the question instead of leaving it open indefinitely; if any operational script, migration runner, or reporting connection ever runs as the table owner against production data, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY must be set on every RLS-enabled table before that access pattern ships.
findings.why: Postgres's own documented default is that a table's OWNER role bypasses its own RLS policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is explicitly set; this is a genuinely surprising default (most people assume 'RLS enabled' means 'RLS always applies') and it is exactly the shape of silent-hole this whole file researches. Leaving it as an open, unverified question forever costs nothing until the day someone adds an operational script, a reporting connection, or a data-migration tool that happens to connect as the table owner, at which point every RLS policy in the project silently does nothing for that connection and nobody would know without already knowing to check this specific thing.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rn 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' supabase/migrations -> zero hits across all 269+ migration files, confirming (this session, not just 'unverified' as research/authz.md left it) that no table in this project has ever had FORCE RLS applied. _inventory/_db-snapshot.json (capturedAt: 2026-07-12, 146 tables, rlsDisabled: []) confirms ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is universal, which is the weaker guarantee Postgres's own docs warn does not bind the owner role.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' supabase/migrations/*.sql -> 0 hits (upgraded from research/authz.md's own 'Unverified' section, which only speculated this might be missing; this session confirms it is). grep -rn 'relforcerowsecurity\|table owner\|BYPASSRLS.*owner' _backend-system _docs -> zero hits describing which Postgres role Solen's session client actually connects as, so the second half of the open question (does it matter) also remains genuinely unanswered, not just under-documented.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: research/authz.md's own 'Unverified' section already names both halves of this question almost verbatim and correctly frames FORCE RLS as low-priority-but-real. This finding upgrades the first half (is FORCE RLS set) from speculation to a confirmed grep result and leaves the second half (session-client role identity) exactly as open as before, since that requires a live database query this read-only research pass cannot run.
findings.where_it_should_live: a one-line entry in _backend-system/LAW.md once the live-DB check is run (a Supabase/Postgres session, not this read-only pass, would run `SELECT rolname, rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname IN ('anon','authenticated','service_role')` and `SELECT tableowner FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname='public' LIMIT 1` to close this for good).
findings.enforcement: checklist: a one-time live-DB verification task, not a recurring gate (Supabase's setup is stable enough that this does not need periodic re-checking, only re-checking if the connection architecture ever changes).

findings.title: The one admin-impersonation-shaped route writes no audit trail, despite an existing, used audit_log table and 26 other admin routes doing so
findings.principle: Any route that lets one identity act as, view as, or preview data scoped to another identity (an admin previewing a salon's dashboard, a future 'view as this customer' support tool) must write an audit_log row (actor id, target id/type, action name, timestamp) at the moment of that access, using the same logAuditEvent() helper every other privileged admin action in this codebase already uses, before the feature's scope is ever widened beyond a narrow, low-risk starting case.
findings.why: Impersonation is the one authorization pattern where 'the check passed' is not the end of the story: even a correctly role-gated, correctly scoped impersonation grants visibility into another party's data, and the only backstop against that capability being misused (not attacked, misused, by a legitimate admin acting outside their remit) is a durable, admin-visible-to-all record of who did it, to whom, when, and ideally why. A capability with no audit trail is a private backdoor even when its access control is otherwise perfect, because 'perfect access control' only proves the RIGHT PEOPLE can use it, not that they always should.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/admin/preview-salon/route.ts is correctly role-gated (admin only) and correctly scoped (restricted to [TEST]%-prefixed salons only, a 1-hour cookie), but never calls lib/audit.ts's logAuditEvent(), the exact helper 26 other admin routes (salon approve/reject/freeze/warn, commission changes, feature-flag toggles, discovery moderation) already call for actions of comparable or lower sensitivity. Today this is low-risk specifically because the route is scoped to test salons only, meaning no real customer/salon data is exposed by it yet, but a support-tooling feature request to 'preview a REAL salon's dashboard to debug an issue' is a natural, likely next step, and it would inherit this same silent-audit-trail gap unless it's closed first.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'logAuditEvent' app/api/admin/preview-salon/route.ts -> zero hits (confirmed by direct read of the full file, not just a grep). grep -rn 'audit_log\|logAuditEvent' app/api/admin/preview-salon -> zero hits.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: this exact gap is already named, with the exact fix (one line: await logAuditEvent(request, user.id, "preview_salon", "salon", salon_id)), in audit/authn.md as AUTHN-12 (severity LOW, given the test-salon-only scoping). It is filed under the authn audit rather than an authz one, which is a reasonable categorization (impersonation sits at the authn/authz boundary) but means it is easy to miss if a future session only reads authz.md and assumes impersonation is out of scope there.
findings.where_it_should_live: the fix itself belongs in app/api/admin/preview-salon/route.ts (a one-line addition, already scoped and named); the LAW-level principle ('any impersonation-shaped route must audit-log at access time') belongs in _backend-system/LAW.md's authz section so it binds the NEXT impersonation feature too, not just this one route.
findings.enforcement: gate: extend no-unauth-money-route.py's sibling-gate pattern, or a new small hook, to flag a new route.ts under app/api/admin/ that reads another user's/salon's row by id (a preview/impersonate/view-as shape) without a logAuditEvent( call in the same file.
